chunks: Highest frequency in real vs ideal square wave. The question: What is the highest frequency component of a real vs ideal square wave?
Any repeating wave can be built by adding sine waves, the smooth, evenly wavy signal from math class.
An ideal square wave has instant edges, and an instant jump takes sine waves of ever higher frequency, without end. So it has no highest frequency.
A real square wave's edges take some time, so its high-frequency content fades quickly, and the edge speed sets where it stops mattering.
Imagine drawing a shape with marker pens. A rounded corner can be drawn with one thick marker. A perfectly sharp corner needs thinner and thinner pens, forever.
The sine waves are the pens: the thickest draws the basic shape, finer ones add detail. Even a rounded real edge has a little finer detail left. It just stops mattering.
The ideal envelope keeps falling at -20 decibels/decade forever. The real edge follows it up to about 300 megahertz and then plunges at -40 decibels/decade, with periodic nulls.
Near 2 gigahertz the ideal envelope is still at about -20 dBV, while the 1 nanoseconds edge's lobe peaks are near -36 dBV (2 gigahertz itself is one of its nulls).
Against a -60 dBV floor (1 millivolts) the real envelope is below it above about 8 gigahertz, while the ideal one would not reach it until about 200 gigahertz.
The mathematical series is still infinite; the useful bandwidth is not.
Square wave: a signal that switches between two levels at a steady rate ("What a square wave is and its properties").
Harmonic: a sine wave at a whole-number multiple of the square wave's frequency. A square wave uses the 1st, 3rd, 5th and so on.
Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from 10% to 90% of its full height. Highest significant frequency: where the content becomes too weak to matter.
It is a choice, not a fixed fact. Rule of thumb: about 0. 35 divided by the rise time gives that frequency ("Rule of thumb for real square wave bandwidth").
Take a 100 megahertz clock with 1 nanoseconds edges. The rule gives 0.
35 / 1 nanoseconds = 350 megahertz, so the important content stops around the 3rd harmonic (300 megahertz) or the 5th (500 megahertz). Harmonics beyond that are weak.
Now slow the clock to 10 megahertz but keep the same 1 nanoseconds edges. The important content still reaches about 350 megahertz, which is roughly the 35th harmonic.
The clock rate changed tenfold. The reach did not. That is the whole idea: the edge, not the clock rate, sets the highest frequency that matters.
"An ideal square wave has instant edges, so it contains harmonics out to infinity, falling only as one over n. A real one has a finite rise time.

It still has infinitely many harmonics mathematically, but above a knee of about one over pi times the rise time they fall off at 40 decibels per decade, and real drivers and traces low-pass it further.
So the highest significant frequency is set by the edge, roughly 0. 35 to 0. 5 over the rise time, not by the clock frequency."
